book_title:
The Book of Proverbs,
which the Hebrews call Misle. משלי

intros.title: THE ARGUMENT OF THE PROVERBS.
intros.text: The first book called Proverbs, that is, common & usual pithy sentences, short in words, ample in [1] sense; and Parables, signifying likeness or similitudes, whereby more important things are understood than expressed; instructeth and exhorteth new beginners, to learn, and practise all sorts of virtues, the only right way to true wisdom and eternal happiness. It may be divided [2] into four parts. In the first nine chapters the author interposing certain general precepts, [3] produceth wisdom herself inviting all men to seek her, for the spiritual profit, they shall thereby enjoy. From thence to the 25. chap. he giveth sundry more particular precepts, as well for embracing virtues, as shunning of vices. In the next five chapters, more like precepts of the same author, are added by the care of King Ezechias. In the thirtieth chapter, either another Author, or rather the same under another title, and in prophetical style, uttereth like divine sentences; adding in the last chapter, other excellent precepts received of his mother: whereto he adjoineth the praise of a right wise woman; prophetically the Catholic Church.

notes.text: Why this book is called Proverbs and Parables.

intros.title: THE THIRD PART OF THE OLD TESTAMENT CONTAINING SAPIENTIAL BOOKS.
intros.text: The argument of Sapiential Books. Hitherto the Law and History of God's peculiar people are set forth in the former parts of the holy Bible: after which followed the Book of psalms, which in manner of style, being all in verse, is a distinct part, but in substance of matter, is an Epitome or brief Sum of all holy Scripture: most conveniently therefore placed in the midst of the rest, as the Sun amongst other Planets, a shining great light in a large house. Now ensueth the third part, containing Divine Instructions, or [1] Rules of good life. A doctrine most agreeable to God's high wisdom, and most fitly commended to Man, his reasonable creature in earth. But besides the principal subject, as before is noted (that each part participated with others in their proper contents) so here be many precepts of [2] [3] the Law renewed, sundry examples of men, and things past repeated, and diverse prophecies uttered of things to come: though in this part more specially is shewed the ground, and as it were, the very life or soul of the Law. Which is Reason, the true Rule or Directory wherein all good laws are grounded. For it both sheweth what ought to be done, or avoided, & directeth man's judgment to embrace that is good, and to fly from all evil: not only illuminating the understanding to see that is right and just, but also disposing the internal affection to desire, love, choose, and prefer the right path of God's law, before whatsoever otherwise seemeth pleasant or profitable: & so, not withstanding all dangers, difficulties, distresses, worldly calamities, and death itself, effectually persuading to persevere to the end in holy conversation. All which by a general name is called Wisdom: ◦ comprising in one word, all good desires, holy virtues, supernal gifts, godly endeavours, and the whole means whereby God is rightly known, & duly served, whereof these five Books, teaching this most excellent and most necessary manner of life, are called Sapiential. Nevertheless four of them have also other particular names, as appeareth in their titles. Only the fourth is called the Book of Wisdom, by appropriation of the general name. All five are Canonical and assured holy Scripture: as is shewed before, and may be further [4] [5] proved of the two later, which Protestants deny. It is also evident that King Salomon was [6] Author of the three former: as S. Jerome, S. Augustin, and other Fathers prove by the holy text [7] itself. It is likewise certain that he either writ, or at least by divine inspiration uttered, much more than is now extant. For the holy Scripture (3. Reg. 4.) testifieth that he spake three thousand [8] Parables: and his Songs were a thousand and five. He disputed of the trees from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop which cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and fowls, and creeping worms, and fishes. Josephus (li. 8. c. 2. Antiq.) following some other Edition, saith his songs were five thousand, and parables (as the ordinary text hath) three thousand. For he deduced a parable (saith Josephus) throughout every kind of trees, from the hyssop to the cedar. In the same manner he treated of beasts, and other living creatures of the earth, water, and air. For he was not ignorant of any natural thing, neither omitted to treat thereof, but clearly explicated all their natural properties. Most briefly S. Jerome declareth both the Author and matter of these [9] three books, saying: Salomon the peaceable, and amiable of our Lord correcteth manners: [10] [11] teacheth the nature (of creatures) joineth the Church and Christ; and singeth the sweet [12] [13] bridal song of the holy Marriage.

verses.text: THE Parables of Salomon, the sonne of Dauid, king of Israel.
<na>(a)</na> To know wisdom, and discipline:

notes.label: a
notes.text: By these sentencious similitudes the studious may better conceiue and vnderstand true vvisdom, and the vertues belonging therto.

verses.text: to vnderstand the wordes of prudence: and to receiue instruction of doctrine, iustice, and iudgement, and equitie:
that <na>(b)</na> subtilitie may be geuen to litle ones, knowlege and vnderstanding to the youngman.
The <na>(c)</na> wise man hearing shal be wiser: and he that vnderstandeth, <na>(d)</na> shal possesse gouernementes.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Not only yongmen and inexperienced but also the vvise may lerne more vvisdom by these parables.

notes.label: d
notes.text: shal be fitte to gouerne others.

verses.text: He shal vnderstand a parable, and interpretation, the wordes of the wise, and their darke sayings.
The <na>(e)</na> feare of our Lord is the begynning of wisdom. Fooles despise wisedom and doctrine.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Feare of our Lord, that is, reuerence of his diuine Maiestie vvith desire duly to serue him, and neuer to offend him, is the first degree in ascending to perfect vvisdom : vvhich consisteth not only in the vnderstanding but also in action.

verses.text: My sonne, <na>(f)</na> heare the discipline of thy father, and leaue not the lawe of thy mother:

notes.label: f
notes.text: The first precept is to lerne of our elders.

verses.text: that grace may be added to thy head, and a cheyne of gold to thy necke.
My sonne, <na>(g)</na> if sinners shal entise thee, condescend not to them.

notes.label: g
notes.text: The second to resist euil suggestions.

verses.text: If they shal say: Come with vs, let vs lye in waite for bloud, let vs hide snares against the innocent without cause:
let vs swalow him aliue as hel, and whole as one descending into the lake.
We shal finde al precious substance, we shal fil our house with spoiles.
Cast in thy lot with vs, let there be one purse of vs al.
My sonne, walke not with them, stay thy foote from their pathes.
For their feete runne to euil, and make haste to shede bloud.
But <na>(h)</na> a nette is cast in vayne before the eies of them that haue winges.

notes.label: h
notes.text: The proper remedie against such alurements is to be vvatchful, and to flee from them.

verses.text: Themselues also lye in wayte against their owne bloud & practise deceites against their owne soules.
So the pathes of euerie couetous man, take violently the soules of the possessors.
Wisdom preacheth abrode, she geueth her voice in the streates:
In the head of multitudes she cryeth, in the doores of the gates of the citie she vttereth her wordes, saying:
O children how long doe you loue infancie, and fooles couet those thinges, which are hurtful to them selues, and the vnwise hate knowlege?
Turne ye at my correction: behold I wil vtter my spirite to you, and wil shewe you my wordes.
Because I called, and you refused: I streched out my hand, and there was none that regarded.
You haue despised al my counsel, and haue neglected my reprehensions.
I also wil laugh in your destruction, and wil scorne, when that shal come to you, which you feared.
When soden calamitie shal fal on you, and destruction, as a tempest shal be at hand: when tribulation, and distresse shal come vpon you:
Then shal they inuocate me, and I wil not heare: in the morning shal they arise, and shal not finde me:
for that they haue hated discipline, and not receiued the feare of our Lord,
nor consented to my counsel, & detracted from al my correction.
They shal eate therefore the fruites of their way, and shal be filled with their owne counsels.
The auersion of litle ones shal kil them, and the prosperitie of fooles shal destroy them.
But he that shal heare me, shal rest without terrour, and shal enioy abundance, feare of euils being taken away.

chapters.summary: Parables are profitable to those that loue and wil lerne wisdom. 10. Al are admonished not to folow the alurements of sinners: 20. but to embrace wisdome; 24. and ruine is threatned to the contemners. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text: The first part. And invitation to seek wisdom: with some general precepts.

verses.text: MY sonne, <na>(a)</na> if thou wilt receiue my wordes, and wilt hide my commandments with thee,

notes.label: a
notes.text: This frequent maner of proposing the vvay and meanes to vvisdom If thou vvilt receiue my vvordes, &c. shevveth most euidently the povvre of mans free vvil.

verses.text: that thyne eare may heare wisdom: incline thyne hart to knowe prudence.
For if thou shalt cal for wisdom, and incline thyne hart to prudence:
If thou shalt seeke her <na>(b)</na> as money, and as treasures shalt dig her vp:

notes.label: b
notes.text: Not euerie desire, or sleight seeking of vvisdom sufficieth, but such laborious seeking is required, as a couetous man seeketh treasure vvhich he knoweth to be hid in the ground.

verses.text: then shalt thou vnderstand the feare of our Lord, and shalt finde the knowlege of God.
Because our Lord geueth wisdom: and out of his mouth prudence and knowlege.
He wil keepe the saluation of the righteous, & protect them that walke simply
Keeping the pathes of iustice, & garding the wayes of saints.
Then shalt thou vnderstand iustice, and iudgement, and equitie, and euery good path.
<cr>[1]</cr> If wisdom shal enter into thy hart, and knowlege please thy soule:
counsel shal keepe thee, and prudence shal preserue thee,
that thou mayst be deliuered from the euil way, and from the man, that speaketh peruerse thinges:
<na>(c)</na> who leaue the right way, and walke by darke wayes:

notes.label: c
notes.text: A description of peruers sinners especially of heretikes.

verses.text: who are glad when they haue done euil, and reioyce in most wicked thinges:
whose wayes are peruerse, and their steppes infamous.
That thou mayst be deliuered from the strange woman, and from the forener, which mollifieth her wordes,
forsaketh the guide of her youth,
and hath forgotten the couenant of her God. For her house is bowed downe to death, and her pathes to hel.
Al that goe in vnto her, shal not returne neither shal they apprehend the pathes of life.
That thou mayst walke in a good way: and mayst keepe the pathes of the iust.
For they that are right, shal dwel in the earth, and the simple shal continue in it.
But the impious shal be destroyed from the earth: and they that doe vniustly shal be taken away from it.

chapters.summary: Gaining of wisdom bringeth much good, 10. and auoydeth much euil: 16. deliuering from error of Idolaters and Hæretikes.

verses.text: MY sonne, <na>(a)</na> forget not my law, and let thy <na>(b)</na> hart keepe my precepts.

notes.label: a
notes.text: It auaileth litle to heare good instructions, except vve kepe them in memorie.

notes.label: b
notes.text: not in books only but in the hart:

verses.text: For they shal adde to thee length of dayes, and yeares of life, and peace.
Let not <na>(c)</na> mercie and truth leaue thee, put them about thy throte; and write them in the tables of thy hart:
and thou shalt finde grace, and good discipline before God and men.
<na>(d)</na> Haue confidence in our Lord with al thy hart, and leane not vpon thyne owne prudence.

notes.label: d
notes.text: knovv also that al thy streingth is in God, in vvhom thou maist securely trust, not in thyn ovvne prudence.

verses.text: In al thy wayes thinke on him, and he wil direct thy steppes.
Be not wise in thyne owne conceipte: feare God, and depart from euil:
for it shal be health to thy nauil, and watering of thy bones.
Honour our Lord with thy substance, and geue to him of the first of al thy fruites:
and thy barnes shal be replenished with fulnes, and thy presses shal runouer with wine.
My sonne, cast not away the discipline of our Lord: neither doe thou faint when thou art chasteced of him:
<na>(e)</na> for whom our Lord loueth he chasticeth: and as a father in the sonne he pleaseth himself.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Chastisment and tribulation in those that endeuour to serue God, is a signe of his fauour tovvards them; and therfore his other promises vvhich seme to be temporal, are to be vnderstood of the next life.

verses.text: Blessed is the man that findeth wisdom, and floweth with prudence:
better is the purchasing therof then marchandise of siluer, and her fruite then chiefe and the purest gold:
she is more precious then al riches: and al thinges that are desired, are not able to be compared with her.
<na>(f)</na> Length of dayes in her right hand, & in her left hand <na>(g)</na> riches and glorie

notes.label: f
notes.text: God revvardeth as it vvere vvith both handes promising eternal life,

notes.label: g
notes.text: and competent meanes in this life.

verses.text: Her wayes are beautiful wayes, and al her pathes peaceable.
She is a tree of life to them that shal apprehend her: and he that shal hold her is blessed.
Our Lord by wisdom founded the earth, established the heauens by prudence.
By his wisdom the depthes haue broken forth, and the cloudes waxe thicke with dew.
My sonne, let not these thinges depart from thyne eies: kepe the law & counsel:
and there shal be life to thy soule, and <na>(h)</na> grace to thy iawes.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Merite for the vvordes of thy mouth.

verses.text: Then shalt thou walke confidently in thy way, and thy foote shal not stumble:
if thou sleepe, thou shalt not feare: thou shalt rest, and thy sleepe shal be sweete.
Dread not at soden terrour, and the power of the impious falling vpon thee.
For our Lord wil be at thy side, and wil keepe thy foote that thou be not taken.
Doe not prohibite him to doe good, that is able: if thou be able, thy selfe also doe good.
Say not to thy frend: goe, and returne; and <na>(i)</na> to morow I wil geue to thee: wheras thou mayest geue forthwith.

notes.label: i
notes.text: Almes in season is duble vvorth to that vvhich is differred long.

verses.text: Practise not euil against thy freind, when he hath affiance in thee.
Contend not against man without cause, wheras he hath done thee no euil.
Doe not enuie an vniust man, nor imitate his waies:
because euerie deluder is an abomination of our Lord, and his communication is with the simple.
There is pouertie from our Lord in the house of the impious: but the habitations of the iust shal be blessed.
He shal delude the deluders, and to the milde he wil geue grace.
The wise shal possesse glorie: the exaltation of fooles ignominie.

chapters.summary: Wisdom exhorteth to kepe Gods law ( geuing long life ) to obserue mercie, and truth. 5. to confide in God, 7. to feare, 9. and honour him, 11. to take his correction gladly ( 13. for al good thinges folow wisdom ) 27. to releue the needie without delay, 30. not to contend with the wicked, nor to imitate them. 33. The euil shal faile, and the godlie shal prosper.

verses.text: CHILDREN heare ye the fathers discipline, and attend that you may knowe prudence.
I wil geue you a good gift, forsake not my law.
For <na>(a)</na> I also was the sonne of my father, tender and as onlie begotten in my mothers sight:

notes.label: a
notes.text: As Salomon was instructed by his father king Dauid so he teacheth others, the right order novve to lerne vvisdom.

verses.text: and he taught me, & sayd: Let thy hart receiue my wordes, kepe my preceptes, and thou shalt liue.
Possesse wisedom, possesse prudence: forget not, neither decline from the wordes of my mouth.
Leaue her not, and she wil keepe thee: loue her, and she wil preserue thee.
<na>(b)</na> The beginning of wisdom, possesse wisdom, and in al thy possession purchase prudence:

notes.label: b
notes.text: The first part of wisdom it is to desire it. For nothing hindereth from being iust but that iustice is not desired. S. Aug. in Psal. 118. v. 20.

verses.text: take quickly, and she wil exalt thee: thou shalt be glorified of her, when thou shalt embrace her.
She wil geue to thy head increase of graces, and with a noble crowne she wil protect thee.
Heare my sonne, and receiue my wordes, that yeares of life may be multiplied to thee.
The way of wisdom I wil shew to thee, I wil leade thee by the pathes of equitie.
Which when thou shalt haue entered, thy steppes shal not be straytened, and running thou shalt not haue a stumbling blocke.
Hold discipline, leaue it not: kepe it, because the same is thy life.
Be not delighted in the pathes of the impious, neither let the way of the euil please thee.
Flee from it, neither passe thou by it: goe aside, and forsake it.
For they sleepe not vnlesse they haue done il: and they take no sleepe vnlesse they supplant.
They eate the bread of impietie, and drinke the wine of iniquitie.
But the path of the iust, as shyning light proceedeth euen to perfect day.
The way of the impious is darkesom: they know not where they fal.
My sonne, heare my wordes, and incline thyne eare to my sayinges.
Let them not depart from thyne eies, kepe them in the middes of thy hart.
For they are life to those that finde them, and health to al flesh.
With al garde keepe thy <na>(c)</na> hart, because life proceedeth from it.

notes.label: c
notes.text: As the hart is the principal part of the bodie, so the vvil is the chiefest povvre of the soule: from vvhich good or euil procedeth.

verses.text: Remoue from thee a froward mouth, and let detracting lippes be far from thee.
Let thyne eies see right thinges, & let thine eieliddes goe before thy steppes.
Direct the path to thy feete, and al thy wayes shal be established.
Decline not to the right hand, nor to the left: turne away thy foote from euil.
For our Lord knoweth the wayes that are on the right hand: but those are peruers, which are on the left hand.
But he wil make thy courses right, and thy wayes he wil bring forward in peace.

chapters.summary: The wiseman exhorteth others by his owne example to seeke wisdom, 14. to decline from the wicked, and to imitate the iust, 23. to guide wel the hart, mouth, and feete.

verses.text: MY sonne, attend to my wisdom, and to my prudence incline thyne eare,
that thou mayst keepe <na>(a)</na> cogitations, and thy lippes preserue discipline.

notes.label: a
notes.text: To auoide al impietie it is first of al necessarie, not to thinke, speake, nor heare vnlawful thinges.

verses.text: Attend not to the deceipt of a <na>(b)</na> woman: for the lippes of an harlot are as a hony combe distilling, and her throte netter then oyle.

notes.label: b
notes.text: By woman is generally vnderstood concupiscence of vvhat sinne soeuer, as ch. 1. v. 10. & ch 3. v. 33. chap. 4. v. 14.

verses.text: But her later endes are bitter as wormewood, and sharpe as a two edged sword.
Her feete goe downe into death, and her steppes penetrate vnto hel.
They walke not by the path of life, her steppes are wandering, and vnsearcheable.
Now therfore my sonne heare me, and depart not from the wordes of my mouth.
Make thy way far from her, and aproch not to the doores of her house.
Geue not thy honour <na>(c)</na> to strangers, and thy yeres to the <na>(d)</na> cruel.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The vvorld the flesh and the diuel are strangers.

notes.label: d
notes.text: And cruel enemies that render for revvard eternal damnation.

verses.text: Lest perhaps strangers be filled with thy strength, and thy labours be in an other mans house,
and thou mourne in the end, when thou shalt haue spent thy flesh and thy bodie, and say:
Why haue I detested discipline, and my hart consented not to reprehensions,
nor I heard the voice of them that taught me, and haue not inclined mine eare to masters?
I haue almost bene in al euil, in the middes of the church and of the synagoge.
Drinke water of thyne owne cesterne, and the stremes of thy wel:
<na>(e)</na> Let thy fountaines be deriued abrode, and in the streates diuide thy waters.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Good doctrine is to be imperted to men of sincere intention.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> Haue them alone, neither let strangers be partakers with thee.

notes.label: f
notes.text: not to contemners and obstinate infidels.

verses.text: Let thy vayne be blessed, and reioyce with the woman of thy youth:
a hinde most deare, and a most grateful fawne: let her breastes inebriate thee at al time, in her loue be thou delighted continually.
Why art thou seduced my sonne of a strange woman, and art cherished in the bosome of an other?
Our Lord beholdeth the wayes of a man, and considereth al his steppes.
His owne iniquities take the impious, and he is fast bonde with the ropes of his sinnes.
He shal die because he hath not had discipline, and in the multitude of his folie he shal be deceiued.

chapters.summary: Againe wisdom dehorteth from fornication ( carnal and spiritual ) 6. shewing that in the end sinners shal see and feele the effect of their follie: 20. which God seeth and wil punish.

verses.text: MY sonne, <na>(a)</na> if thou shalt be suretie for thy freind, and hast made fast thy hand to a stranger,

notes.label: a
notes.text: The wisman doth not absolutly disswade from al maner of suretishippe, but from rashly, or vnaduisedly answering for others. And especially exhorteth to vse al diligence in performing, or causing others to performe that vvhich is promised or couenanted.

verses.text: thou art entrapped with the wordes of thy mouth, & caught with thyne owne wordes.
Doe therefore my sonne that which I say, and deliuer thyselfe, because thou art fallen into the hand of thy neighbour. Runne diuers wayes, make hast, rayse thy freind:
Geue not sleepe to thine eies, neither let thine eieliddes slumber.
Deliuer thyselfe as a litle doa from the hand, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler.
Goe to the emmote ô sluggard, and consider her wayes, and lerne wisdom.
Who wheras she hath no guide, nor master, nor captaine,
prepareth meate for herselfe in the summer, and gethereth in the haruest for to eate
How long wilt thou sleepe ô sluggard? when wilt thou rise out of thy sleepe?
Thou shalt sleepe a litle, a litle shalt thou slumber, a litle shalt thou ioyne thy handes to sleepe:
and penurie shal come to thee, as a wayfaring man, and pouertie as a man armed. But if thou be not sluggish, thy haruest shal come as a fountaine, and penurie shal flee farre from thee.
A man that is an <na>(b)</na> Apostata, a man vnprofitable, goeth with peruerse mouth,

notes.label: b
notes.text: Euerie one that sinneth vvittingly and of malice refusing to obey God, imployeth his mouth, eies, feete, handes and al partes vvith a wicked hart and intention to peruerte others: most proper to heretikes, apostates from the faith.

verses.text: winketh with the eies, treadeth with the foote, speaketh with the finger,
with wicked hart he deuiseth euil, and at al time he soweth brawles.
To him his destruction shal come forthwith, and he shal sodenlie be destroyed, neither shal he haue remedie any more.
Six thinges there are, which our Lord hateth, and the seuenth his soule detesteth:
Loftie eies, a lying tongue, handes that shede innocent bloud,
a hart that deuiseth most wicked deuises, feete swift to runne into euil,
a deceitful witnesse that vttereth lies, and him that among brether <na>(c)</na> soweth discordes.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The former six are al damnable, but this seuenth is most detestable, because it is opposite to the chief vertue charitie, it breaketh vnitie, & is the proper sinne of the diuel.

verses.text: My sonne keepe the preceptes of thy father, and leaue not the lawe of thy mother.
Bynde them in thy hart continualy, and put them about thy throte.
When thou shalt walke, let them goe with thee: when thou shalt sleepe, let them kepe thee, and awaking talke with them.
Because the commandment is a lampe, and the lawe a light, and the way of life the increpation of discipline:
that they may kepe thee from the euil woman, and from the faire spoken tongue of the stranger.
Let not thy hart couet her beautie, be not caught with her beckes:
for the price of an harlot is scarse worth one loafe: but a woman catcheth the precious soule of man.
<na>(d)</na> Can a man hide fyre in his bosome, that his garmentes burne not?

notes.label: d
notes.text: Al occasions of sinne, especially probable are to be shunned.

verses.text: Or walke vpon hote coales, that his soales be not burnt?
so he that goeth in vnto his neighbours wife, shal not be cleane when he shal touche her.
It is <na>(e)</na> no greate fault, when a man shal haue stollen: for he stealeth to fil his hungrie soule:

notes.label: e
notes.text: Theft is also mortal sinne, against the seuenth cōmandment, but not so great as adulterie.

verses.text: also being taken he shal restore seuenfold, and shal geue vp al the substance of his house.
But he that is an aduouterer, for penurie of hart shal destroy his owne soule:
shame and ignominie he gethereth to himselfe, & his reproch shal not be blotted out.
Because the zele and furie of the husband wil not spare in the day of reuenge,
neither wil he yeld to any mans prayers, neither wil he take for redemption verie many giftes.

chapters.summary: He that is suretie for an other, must haue care to discharge that he promiseth. 6. The slouthful must lerne diligence of the emmotte. 12. The description of an Apostata. 16. Aboue other six bad thinges, God detesteth the sower of discord. 20. Al are exhorted to kepe Gods law, 24. namely to flee fornication, and al occasions therof.

verses.text: MY sonne, <na>(a)</na> keepe my wordes, and my preceptes hide with thee. Sonne,

notes.label: a
notes.text: Because tentations stil occurre in this life, and man is fraile, good exhortations, and earnest admonitions must also be continualy inculcated, as here the vvisman often repeteth and much vrgeth the same good and necessarie aduises to embrace vvisdom and to vvalke stil in the vvay of vertue, especially to flee from vices, and dangers of sinne.

verses.text: keepe my commandmentes, and thou shalt liue: and my law as the apple of thine eie:
binde it on thy fingers, write it in the tables of thy hart.
Say to wisdom, thou art my sister: & cal prudence thy freind,
that she may keepe thee from the strange woman, and from the forener which maketh her wordes sweete.
For out of the window of my house I looked out through the lattise,
and I see litle ones, I behold a foolish youngman,
which passeth through the streates by the corner, and goeth nigh the way of her house,
in the darke the day being toward euening, in the darkenes of the night, and dimnes,
And behold the woman meeteth him in harlotes atyre, prepared to deceiue soules: babling and wandering,
impatient of rest, nor able to consist in the house on her feete,
now abrode, now in the streates, now lying in wayte neere the corners.
And taking the youngman she kisseth him, and with malepert countenance speaketh fayre, saying:
I vowed victimes for welfare, this day I haue payed my vowes.
Therfore I am come forth to meete thee, desirous to see thee, and I haue found thee.
I haue wouen my bed with cordes, I haue adorned it with tapestrie pictured out of Ægypt.
I haue sprinkled my bed with myrrhe, aloes, and cinamome.
Come let vs be inebriated with brestes, and let vs enioy desired embracings, til the day appeare.
For my husband is not at home, he is gone a very long iourney.
he caried with him a bagge of money: in the day of the ful moone he wil returne to his house.
She intangled him with many wordes, and with flatterie of lippes drewe him.
Immediatly he foloweth her <na>(b)</na> as an oxe led to be a victime, & as a lambe playing the wanton, and not knowing that he is drawen as a foole to bondes,

notes.label: b
notes.text: Sinners after consent geuen to tentations, are as inconsiderate of their owne state, & of their perile and ruine, as an oxe, vvhen he is ledde to the shamles, or a bird allured vvith a bate, that flieth into the snare or nette.

verses.text: til the arow pearse his liuer: as if a birde should make haste to the snare, and knoweth not that his life is in danger.
Now therfore my sonne, heare me, and attend to the wordes of my mouth.
Let not thy mind be drawen away in her wayes: neither be thou deceiued with her pathes.
For she hath cast downe manie wounded, and al the most strong are slaine by her.
Her house the wayes of hel, penetrating to the inner partes of death.

chapters.summary: He further exhorteth yongmen to seke wisdom, 5. especially to flee from the intisements of harlots, largely describing the same, 22. and the ruine of them that are so deluded.

verses.text: DOTH not wisdom crie, and prudence geue her voice?
Standing <na>(a)</na> in the high & loftie toppes ouer the way, in the middes of the pathes,

notes.label: a
notes.text: True wisdom directing to good life, & so to eternal saluation, is only found in the visible Church standing vpon a mountaine, not hidde in corners or obscure places.

verses.text: beside the gates of the citie, in the verie doores she speaketh, saying:
O men, to you I crie, and my voice is to the children of men.
O litle ones vnderstand subtiltie, and ye vnwise marke.
Heare ye, because I wil speake of great thinges: and my lippes shal be opened to preach right thinges.
My throte shal meditate truth, and my lippes shal detest the impious.
Al my wordes are iust, there is no wicked, nor peruerse thing in them.
They are right to them that vnderstand, and iust to them that finde knowlege.
Receiue ye discipline, & not money: choose doctrine rather then gold.
For wisdom is better then al most precious riches: and whatsoeuer is to be desired can not be compared to it.
I <na>(b)</na> wisdome dwel in counsel, and am present in lerned cogitations.

notes.label: b
notes.text: These singular praises perteine to the increated wisdom, God himself, from whom procedeth wisdom geuen to men by the Holie Ghost. See Annot. ch. 1. v. 2.

verses.text: The feare of our Lord hateth euil: arrogancie, and pride, and wicked way, and a duble roungued mouth I doe detest.
Myne is counsel & equitie, prudence is mine, strength is mine.
By me kinges doe reigne, and the makers of law decree iust thinges.
By me princes rule, and the mightie decree iustice.
I loue them that loue me: and they that watch toward me shal finde me.
With me are riches, and glorie, glorious riches, and iustice.
For my fruite is better then gold, and precious stone, and my blosomes then chosen siluer.
I walke in the wayes of iustice, in the middes of the pathes of iudgement,
that I may enriche them that loue me, and may replenish their treasures.
Our Lord possessed me in the beginning of his wayes, before he had made any thing from the beginning.
From eternitie I was ordayned & of old before the earth was made.
The depthes were not as yet, and I was now conceiued, neither had the fountaines of waters as yet gushed forth:
the mountaines with heauie hugenesse stoode not as yet: before the litle hilles I was brought forth:
he had not yet made the earth, and the riuers, and the poles of the round world.
When he prepared the heauens, I was present: when with a certaine law, and circuite he compassed the depthes:
When he established the firmament aboue, & poysed the fountaines of waters:
when he compassed the sea with her limites, and set a law to the waters that they should not passe their boundes: when he hanged the foundations of the earth.
I was with him, framing al thinges: and was delighted euerie day, playing before him at al time;
playing in the world: & <na>(c)</na> my delights to be with the children of men.

notes.label: c
notes.text: God much preferreth man before al other corporal creatures.

verses.text: Now therfore children heare me: blessed are they, that keepe my wayes.
Heare ye discipline, and be wise, and reiect it not.
Blessed is the man that heareth me, & that watcheth at my doores dayly, & wayteth at the postes of my doore.
He that shal finde me, shal finde life, and shal draw saluation of our Lord:
but he that shal sinne against me, shal hurt his owne soule. Al that hate me, loue death.

chapters.summary: Wisdom is preached in conspicuous and most frequented places, that none may pretend wante of admonition, 7. her doctrin is true, godlie, profitable, & necessarie to al sortes of men. 12. wisdom (increated which is God himselfe) is eternal. 32. and bringeth eternal happines.

verses.text: banquet of stollen water and hidde bread.
WISEDOME hath built herself an house, she hath cut out seuen pillers.
She hath immolated her victimes, mingled her wine, and set forth her table.
She hath sent her handmaides to cal to the towre, and to the walles of the citie:
If any be a litle one, let him come to me. And to the vnwise she spake:
Come, <na>(a)</na> eate ye my bread, & drinke the wine which I haue mingled for you.

notes.label: a
notes.text: S. Cyprian li. 1. ep. 3. citeth this whole passage of Christs Sacrifice in the formes of bread and wine.

verses.text: Leaue infancie, and liue, and walke by the wayes of prudence.
He that teacheth a scorner doth iniurie to himself; and he that rebuketh the impious, purchaseth a blotte to himself.
Rebuke <na>(b)</na> not the scorner lest hee hate thee. <na>(c)</na> Rebuke a wise man, and he wil loue thee.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Where is no hope of amendment prudence directeth vs not to admonish, nor rebuke sinners, lest without anie fruite we procure emnitie. charitie also requireth rather to expect better opportunitie, lest the offender become worse by our admonition.

notes.label: c
notes.text: But when there is hope of good, euerie one is bond, especially superiors to correct offenders. S. Aug. li. 1. c. 9. de ciuit. S. Basil. regulis fuse disput. 158.

verses.text: Geue occasion to a wise man, and wisdom shal be added to him. Teach the iust, and he shal make haste to take it.
The beginning of wisdom, the feare of our Lord: and the knowlege of the holie, prudence.
For by me shal thy dayes be multiplied, and yeres of life shal be added to thee.
If thou be wise, to thyself thou shalt be: and if a scorner, thou alone shalt beare the euil.
A foolish woman and clamorous, and ful of alurementes, and knowing nothing at al,
sate in the doores of her house vpon a seate in a high place of the citie,
to cal them that passe by the way, and goe on their iourney:
He that is a litle one, let him turne to me. And to the foole she spake:
Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant.
and he was ignorant that giantes are there, and her guestes in the depthes of hel.

chapters.summary: Wisdom hauing built her house with seuen pillers, inuiteth al to a prepared banquette, 11. promising to multiplie ioyful dayes. 13. Folie inciteth to her contrarie

verses.text: A wise sonne maketh the father glad: but a foolish sonne is the sorow of his mother. <na>[1]</na>
The treasures of impietie shal profit nothing: but iustice shal deliuer from death. <na>[1]</na>
Our Lord wil not afflict with famine the soule of the iust, and the deceitful practises of the impious he wil ouerthrow. <na>[1]</na>

The slothful hand hath wrought pouertie: the hand of the strong getteth riches. <na>[1]</na> Who so trusteth to lyes feedeth the windes: and the selfe same man foloweth the flying birdes. <na>[2]</na>
He that gathereth in the haruest, is a wise sonne: but he that snorteth in summer, is the sonne of confusion. <na>[1]</na>
The blessing of our Lord is vpon the head of the iust: but iniquitie couereth the mouth of the impious. <na>[1]</na>
The memorie of the iust is with prayses: and the name of the impious shal rotte. <na>[1]</na>
The wise of hart shal receiue preceptes: a foole is beaten with lippes. <na>[1]</na>
He that walketh playnly, walketh confidently: but he that depraueth his wayes, shal be manifest. <na>[1]</na>
He that wincketh with the eye, shal geue sorow: and the foole in lippes shal be beaten. <na>[1]</na>
A vayne of life, the mouth of the iust: and the mouth of the impious couereth iniquitie. <na>[1]</na>
Hatred rayseth brawles: and charitie couereth al sinnes. <na>[1]</na>
In the lippes of the wise wisdom is found: and a rod on his backe that lacketh witte. <na>[1]</na>
Wise men hide knowlege: but the mouth of the foole is next to confusion. <na>[1]</na>
The substance of a rich man, is a citie of his strength: the feare of the poore their pouertie. <na>[1]</na>
The worke of the iust vnto life: but the fruite of the impious vnto sinne. <na>[1]</na>
The way of life, to him that keepeth discipline: but he that forsaketh reprehensions, erreth. <na>[1]</na>
Lying lippes hide hatred; he that vttereth contumelie is vnwise. <na>[1]</na>
In much talke there shal not want sinne: but he that moderateth his lippes is most wise. <na>[1]</na>
The tongue of the iust, is chosen siluer: but the hart of the impious is nothing worth. <na>[1]</na>
The lippes of the iust teach verie many: but they that are vntaught, shal die in the penurie of witte. <na>[1]</na>
The blessing of our Lord maketh men rich: neither shal affliction be ioyned to them. <na>[1]</na>
A foole worketh mischeefe as it were by laughter: but wisdom is prudence to a man. <na>[1]</na>
That which the impious feareth, shal come vpon him: to the iust their desire shal be geuen. <na>[1]</na>
As a tempest passing the impious shal not be: but the iust as an euerlasting fundation. <na>[1]</na>
As vinegre to the teeth, and smoke to the eies, so a sluggard to them, that sent him. <na>[1]</na>
The feare of our Lord shal adde dayes: and the yeares of the impious shal be shortened. <na>[1]</na>
The expectation of the iust is ioy: but the hope of the impious shal perish. <na>[1]</na>
The strength of the simple the way of our Lord: and feare is to them that worke euil. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Obseruation of Gods law, fulfulling al iustice.

verses.text: The iust for euer shal not be moued: but the impious shal not dwel on the earth.
The mouth of the iust shal bring forth wisdom: the tongue of the froward shal perish. <na>[1]</na>
The lippes of the iust consider gratful thinges: and the mouth of the impious peruerse thinges.

articles.title: THE PARABLES OF SALOMON.
articles.text: This repetition of the title signifieth, that the sentences which follow are more properly called <mn>[1]</mn> Parables, than the former: From which they also differ in manner of utterance, by the figure Antithesis, for most part opposing, and comparing contrary virtues and vices, shewing their contrary effects; with great elegancy, especially in the original tongue; which could not be so fully expressed in Greek, nor Latin, much less in vulgar language: But are the same in sense, though <mn>[2]</mn> often obscure, by reason of the Hebrew phrase, shortness of sentences, and so without any certain connexion, that we cannot with perspicuity, comprehend the sum thereof in brief contents, after the ordinary manner before the chapters. And therefore have thought it better for the vulgar reader, to set down in the margent of the twenty chapters next following, in brief terms, the <mn>[3]</mn> virtues, or other good things (rather than the bad, not having place for both) commended in every sentence. For though the same be not always expressed in the text, yet they may be understood by their opposite vices. Whosoever desireth further explication, may find many of these divine sentences excellently expounded by S. Jerome. S. Augustine, S. Gregory and other Fathers in several places. Or read S. Beda's Commentaries upon this whole book, To. 4. Vel apud S. Jerome. To. 7. Or amongst late writers, our learned countryman D. Radulphus Bainus, Bishop Jansenius, and F. Peltanus.

notes.text: The second part. Sententious moral precepts.
How these Parables following differ from the former.
Why the contents of the twenty chapters following are put in the margent.

verses.text: A deceitful balance, is abomination before God: and an equal weight is his wil. <na>[1]</na>
Where pride shal be, there shal be contumelie also: but where humilitie, there also wisdom. <na>[1]</na>
The simplicitie of the iust shal direct them: and the supplanting of the peruers shal waste them. <na>[1]</na>
Riches shal not profit in the day of reuenge: but iustice shal deliuer from death. <na>[1]</na>
The iustice of the simple shal direct his way: and the impious shal fal in his impietie. <na>[1]</na>
The iustice of the righteous shal deliuer them: and the vniust shal be caught in their deceitful practises. <na>[1]</na>
The impious man being dead, there shal be no hope any more: and the expectation of the careful shal perish. <na>[1]</na>
The iust is deliuered from distresse: and the impious shal be geuen for him. <na>[1]</na>
The dissembler with his mouth deceiueth his freind: but the iust shal be deliuered by knowlege. <na>[1]</na>
In the good thinges of the iust the citie shal reioyce; and in the destruction of the impious there shal be prayse. <na>[1]</na>
With the benediction of the iust the citie shal be exalted: and by the mouth of the impious it shal be subuerted. <na>[1]</na>
He that despiseth his freind, lacketh hart: but the wise man wil hold his peace. <na>[1]</na>
He that walketh fraudulently, reueleth secretes: but he that is faithful, concealeth the thing comitted of his freind. <na>[1]</na>
Where there is no gouernour, the people shal fal: but there is health where is much counsel. <na>[1]</na>
He shal be afflicted with euil, that is suretie for a stranger: but he that is ware of the snares, shal be secure. <na>[1]</na>
A gracious woman shal finde glorie: and the strong shal haue riches. <na>[1]</na>
A merciful man doth good to his kinred also. <na>[1]</na>
The impious maketh an vnstable worke: but to him that soweth iustice, is a faythful reward. <na>[1]</na>
Clemencie prepareth life: & the pursewing of euil thinges death. <na>[1]</na>
A peruers hart is abominable to our Lord: and his wil is in them that walke simply. <na>[1]</na>
Hand in hand the euil man shal not be innocent: but the seede of the iust shal be saued. <na>[1]</na>
A ring of gold in a swines snoute, a fayre woman & a foole. <na>[1]</na>
The desire of the iust is al good: the expectation of the impious furie. <na>[1]</na>
Some diuide their owne goodes, and are made richer: others take violently not their owne, and are alwayes in pouertie. <na>[1]</na>
The soule which blesseth, shal be made fatte: and he that inebriateth himself shal also be inebriated. <na>[1]</na>
He that hydeth corne, shal be cursed among the peoples: but blessing vpon the head of them that sel. <na>[1]</na>
Wel riseth he early who seeketh good thinges: but he that is a searcher after euil thinges, shal be oppressed of them. <na>[1]</na>
He that trusteth in his riches shal fal: but the iust shal spring as a greene leafe. <na>[1]</na>
He that troubleth his house, shal possesse the windes: and he that is a foole shal serue the wise. <na>[1]</na>
The fruite of the iust man a tree of life: and he that gaineth soules, is wise. <na>[1]</na>
If the iust man receiue in the earth, how much more the impious and sinner? <na>[1]</na>
HE that loueth discipline, loueth knowlege: but he that hateth reprehensions is vnwise. <na>[1]</na>
He that is good, shal draw grace from our Lord: but he that trusteth in his owne cogitation, doth impiously. <na>[1]</na>
Man shal not be strengthened by impietie: and the roote of the iust shal not be moued. <na>[1]</na>
A diligent woman is a crowne to her husband: and putrefaction in his bones, she that doth thinges worthie of confusion. <na>[1]</na>
The cogitations of the iust are iudgements: & the counsels of the impious are fraudulent. <na>[1]</na>
The wordes of the impious lie in wayte for bloud: the mouth of the iust shal deliuer them. <na>[1]</na>
Turne the impious, and they shal not be: but the house of the iust shal be permanent. <na>[1]</na>
A man shal be knowen by his doctrine: but he that is vaine and foolish, shal lye open to contempt. <na>[1]</na>
Better is the poore and sufficient to himself, then he that is glorious and wanteth bread. <na>[1]</na>
The iust knoweth the liues of his beastes: but the bowels of the impious are cruel. <na>[1]</na>

He that tilleth his land, shal be filled with breads: but he that purseweth idlenes is a verie foole. <na>[1]</na> He that is delighted in much quaffing of wine, leaueth contumelie in his munitions. <na>[2]</na>
The desire of the impious is the <na>[1]</na> muniment of the most wicked: but the roote of the iust shal prosper. <na>[2]</na>

notes.text: defence · Iust punishment of the wicked.

verses.text: For the sinnes of the lippes ruine approcheth to the euil man: but the iust escapeth out of distresse. <na>[1]</na>
Of the fruite of his owne mouth shal euerie man be replenished with good thinges, and according to the workes of his handes it shal be repayed him. <na>[1]</na>
The way of a foole is right in his eies: but he that is wise heareth counsels. <na>[1]</na>
A foole by & by sheweth his anger: but he that dissembleth iniuries is wise. <na>[1]</na>
He that speaketh that which he knoweth, is an vtterer of iustice: but he that lyeth, is a fraudulent witnesse. <na>[1]</na>
There is that promiseth, and is pricked as it were with the sword of conscience: but the tongue of the wise is health. <na>[1]</na>
The lippe of truth shal be stable for euer: but he that is an hastie witnesse, frameth a tongue of lying. <na>[1]</na>
Guile is in the hart of them that thinke euil thinges: but ioy foloweth them that geue counsels of peace. <na>[1]</na>
It shal not make the iust sorie what soeuer shal fal to him: but the impious shal be replenished with euil. <na>[1]</na>
Lying lippes are an abomination to our Lord: but they that doe faithfully please him. <na>[1]</na>
A circumspect man concealeth knowlege: and the hart of the vnwise prouoketh folie. <na>[1]</na>
The hand of the strong shal rule, but that which is slothful, shal serue vnder tributes. <na>[1]</na>
Pensifnesse in the hart of a man shal humble him, & with a good word he shal be made glad. <na>[1]</na>
He that neglecteth damage for a freind, is iust: but the way of the impious shal deceiue them. <na>[1]</na>
The fraudulent man shal not finde gayne: and the substance of a <na>[1]</na> man shal be the price of gold. <na>[2]</na>
In the path of iustice, life: but the byway leadeth to death. <na>[1]</na>
A wise sonne, is the doctrine of the father: but he that is a scorner, heareth not when he is rebuked. <na>[1]</na>
Of the fruite of his owne mouth man shal be filled with good thinges: but the soule of the preuaricatours is wicked. <na>[1]</na>
He that kepeth his mouth, kepeth his soule: but he that is vnaduised to speake shal feele euils. <na>[1]</na>
The sluggard wil and wil not: but the soule of them that worke, shal be made fatte. <na>[1]</na>
The iust shal detest a lying word: but the impious confoundeth, and shal be confounded. <na>[1]</na>
Iustice kepeth the way of the innocent: but impietie supplanteth the sinner. <na>[1]</na>
There is one as it were with riches wheras he hath nothing: and there is as it were poore, wheras he is in much riches. <na>[1]</na>
The redemption of a mans life, his riches: but he that is poore, beareth not reprehension. <na>[1]</na>
The light of the iust maketh glad: but the candle of the impious shal be extinguished. <na>[1]</na>
Among the prowde there are alwayes brawles: but they that doe al thinges with counsel, are ruled by wisdom. <na>[1]</na>
Substance hastened shal be diminished: but that which by litle and litle is gathered with the hand, shal be multiplied. <na>[1]</na>
Hope that is differred afflicteth the soule: a tree of life the desire of coming. <na>[1]</na>

Who so detracteth from any thing, he byndeth himselfe for the time to come: but he that feareth the precept, shal conuers in peace. <na>[1]</na> Guilful soules erre in sinnes: the iust are merciful & haue pitie. <na>[2]</na>
The law of a wise man a fountaine of life, that he may decline from the ruine of death. <na>[1]</na>
Good doctrine shal geue grace: in the way of contemners a whirlepoole. <na>[1]</na>
The subtel man doth al thinges with counsel: but he that is a foole openeth folie. <na>[1]</na>
The messenger of the impious shal fal into euil: but a faithful legate, is health. <na>[1]</na>
Pouertie, and ignominie, to him that forsaketh discipline: but he that yeldeth to him that rebuketh, shal be glorified. <na>[1]</na>
Desire if it be accomplished, delighteth the soule: fooles detest them that flee euil thinges. <na>[1]</na>
He that walketh with the wise, shal be wise: a freind of fooles shal be made like. <na>[1]</na>
Euil purseweth sinners, and to the iust good thinges shal be repayed. <na>[1]</na>
The good man leaueth heyres, sonnes and nephewes: and the substance of the sinner is kept for the iust. <na>[1]</na>
Much meate in the tilled growndes of the fathers: and to others they are gathered without iudgement. <na>[1]</na>
He that spareth the rod, hateth his childe: but he that loueth him doth instantly nurture him. <na>[1]</na>
The iust eateth and filleth his soule: but the bellie of the impious vnsatiable. <na>[1]</na>
A wise woman buildeth her house: the vnwise wil with her handes destroy that also which is built. <na>[1]</na>
He that walketh in the right way, & feareth God is despised of him, that goeth an infamous way. <na>[1]</na>
In the mouth of a foole the rod of pride: but the lippes of the wise keepe them. <na>[1]</na>
Where oxen are not, the stal is emptie: but where much corne is, there is the oxes strength manifest. <na>[1]</na>
A faithful witnesse wil not lie: but a deceitful witnesse vttereth a lie. <na>[1]</na>
A scorner seeketh wisdom and findeth it not: the doctrine of the prudent is easie. <na>[1]</na>
Goe against a foolish man, and he knoweth not the lippes of prudence. <na>[1]</na>
The wisdom of a discrete man is to vnderstand his way: and the imprudence of fooles erreth. <na>[1]</na>
A foole wil laugh at sinne, & among the iust grace shal abide. <na>[1]</na>
The hart that knoweth the bitternes of his soule, in his ioy shal not the stranger be mingled. <na>[1]</na>
The house of the impious shal be rased: the tabernacles of the iust shal spring. <na>[1]</na>
There is a way, which seemeth to a man iust: but the later endes therof lead to death. <na>[1]</na>
Laughter shal be mingled with sorow, and mourning occupieth the later endes of ioy. <na>[1]</na>
A foole shal be replenished with his wayes, and the good man shal be aboue him. <na>[1]</na>
The innocent beleueth euerie word: the discrete man considereth his steppes. <na>[1]</na>
A wise man feareth and declineth from euil: the foole leapeth ouer and is confident. <na>[1]</na>
The impatient man shal worke folie: and the subtel man is odious. <na>[1]</na>
<cr>[1]</cr> The childish man shal possesse folie, and the prudent shal expect knowlege. <na>[2]</na>
The euil shal lie downe before the good, and the impious before the gates of the iust. <na>[1]</na>
The poore shal be odious euen to his neighbour: but the freindes of the rich be manie. <na>[1]</na>
He that despiseth his neighbour, sinneth: but he that hath pitie on the poore, shal be blessed. <na>[1]</na>
They erre that worke euil: mercie and truth prepare good thinges. <na>[1]</na>
In euerie worke there shal be abundance: but where manie wordes are, there is oftentimes pouertie. <na>[1]</na>
The crowne of the wise, their riches: the follie of fooles, inprudence. <na>[1]</na>
A faithful witnes deliuereth soules: and the <na>[1]</na> dissembler vttereth lyes. <na>[2]</na>
In the feare of our Lord is confidence of strength, and to his children there shal be hope. <na>[1]</na>
The feare of our Lord a fountaine of life, that he may decline from the ruine of death. <na>[1]</na>
In the multitude of people the dignitie of the king: and in fewnes of people the ignominie of the prince. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Procure loue and fidelitie in subiectes.

verses.text: He that is patient, is gouerned with much wisdom: but he that is impatient, exalteth his follie. <na>[1]</na>
Health of hart, the life of the flesh: enuie, the putrefaction of the bones. <na>[1]</na>
He that doth calumniate the needie, vpbraideth his maker: but he honoreth him, that hath pitie on the poore. <na>[1]</na>
The impious shal be expelled in his malice: but the iust hopeth in his death. <na>[1]</na>
In the hart of the prudent resteth wisdom, & it shal instruct al the vnlerned. <na>[1]</na>
Iustice aduanceth a nation: but sinne maketh peoples miserable. <na>[1]</na>
A seruant that vnderstandeth is acceptable to the king: he that is vnprofitable shal susteyne his anger. <na>[1]</na>
A soft answer breaketh anger: and a hard word rayseth vp furie. <na>[1]</na>
The tongue of the wise adorneth knowlege: the mouth of fooles boyleth forth follie. <na>[1]</na>
In euerie place the eies of our Lord behold the good and the euil. <na>[1]</na>
A peaceable tongue is a tree of life: but that which is immoderate, shal breake the spirite. <na>[1]</na>

A foole scorneth the discipline of his father: but he that regardeth reprehensions, shal become more prudent. <na>[1]</na> In abundant iustice there is greatest force: but the cogitations of the impious shal be rooted out.
The house of the iust is very much strength: and in the fruites of the impious is perturbation. <na>[1]</na>
The lippes of the wise shal sow knowlege: the hart of fooles shal be vnlike. <na>[1]</na>
The victimes of the impious are abominable to our Lord: the vowes of the iust are acceptable. <na>[1]</na>
The way of the impious is abomination to our Lord: he that foloweth iustice is beloued of him. <na>[1]</na>
The doctrine is euil of them that forsake the way of life: he that hateth reprehensions shal dye.
Hel, and perdition are before our Lord: how much more the hartes of the children of men? <na>[1]</na>
The pestilent man loueth not him, that rebuketh him: nor goeth to the wise. <na>[1]</na>
A glad hart cheereth the face: in pensifnes of minde the spirit is cast downe. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: A cherful hart is desirous to lerne.

verses.text: The hart of the wise seeketh doctrine: and the mouth of fooles is fed with vnskilfulnes.
Al the dayes of the poore are euil: a secure minde is as it were a continual feast. <na>[1]</na>
Better is a litle with the feare of our Lord, then great treasures and vnsatiable. <na>[1]</na>
It is better to be called to herbes with charitie: then to a fatted calfe with hatred.
An angrie man stirreth brawles: he that is patient appeaseth those that are raised. <na>[1]</na>
The way of the slothful is as an hedge of thornes: the way of the iust is without offence. <na>[1]</na>
A wise sonne maketh the father ioyful: and the foolish man despiseth his mother. <na>[1]</na>
Follie is ioy to a foole: and the wiseman directeth his steppes. <na>[1]</na>
Cogitations are dissipated where there is no counsel: but where manie counsellers are, they are confirmed. <na>[1]</na>
A man reioyceth in the sentence of his mouth: and a word in due time is best. <na>[1]</na>
The path of life aboue the lerned, that he may decline from the lawest hel. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: To him that is wel trained in good workes, heauen gates are open.

verses.text: Our Lord wil destroy the house of the proude: and wil make sure the borders of the widow.
Euil cogitations are an abomination to our Lord: and pure speach most beautiful shal be confirmed of him. <na>[1]</na>

He that pursueth auarice disturbeth his house: but he that hateth giftes shal liue. <na>[1]</na> By mercie and faith sinnes are purged: and by the feare of our Lord euerie one declineth from euil. <na>[2]</na>
The minde of the iust meditateth obedience: the mouth of the impious redoundeth with euils. <na>[1]</na>
Our Lord is far from the impious: and he wil heare the prayers of the iust. <na>[1]</na>
The light of the eies reioyceth the soule: a good name fatteth the bones. <na>[1]</na>
The eare that heareth the reprehensions of life, shal abide in the middes of the wise. <na>[1]</na>
He that reiecteth discipline, despiseth his soule: but he that yeldeth to reprehensions, is a possessour of the hart. <na>[1]</na>
The feare of our Lord, the discipline of wisdom: and humilitie goeth before glorie. <na>[1]</na>
IT perteyneth to man to prepare the hart: and to our Lord to gouerne the tongue. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Gods grace necessarie in euerie good action.

verses.text: Al the wayes of man are open to his eies: our Lord is the weigher of spirites. <na>[1]</na>
Reueale thy workes to our Lord: and thy cogitations shal be directed. <na>[1]</na>
Our Lord hath wrought al thinges for himself: the impious also to the euil day. <na>[1]</na>

Euerie arrogant man is an abomination to our Lord: although hand shal be to hand he is not <na>[1]</na> innocent. <na>[2]</na> The beginning of a good way, is to doe iustice: and it is more acceptable with God, then to immolate hostes. <na>[3]</na>
By mercie and truth iniquitie is redemed: and in the feare of our Lord euil is auoided. <na>[1]</na>
When the wayes of man shal please our Lord, he wil conuert also his enemies to peace. <na>[1]</na>
Better is a litle with iustice, then much fruite with iniquitie. <na>[1]</na>
The hart of man disposeth his way: but it perteyneth to our Lord to direct his progresse. <na>[1]</na>
<na>[1]</na> Diuination is in the lippes of the king, his mouth shal not erre in iudgement.

notes.text: God assisteth superiors in gouerning their subiectes.

verses.text: Weight and balance are iudgements of our Lord: and his worke al the stones of the bagge. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Iust balance do please God & good kinges.

verses.text: They are abominable to the king that doe impiously: because the throne is established by iustice. <na>[1]</na>
The wil of kinges are iust lippes: he that speaketh right thinges shal be beloued. <na>[1]</na>
The kings indignation, messengers of death: and the wise man wil pacifie it. <na>[1]</na>
In the cherfulnes of the kings countenance is life: and his clemencie is as the later showre.
Possesse wisdom, because it is better then gold: and gette prudence, because it is more precious then siluer. <na>[1]</na>
The path of the iust auoideth euils: the keper of his soule kepeth his way. <na>[1]</na>
Pride goeth before destruction, and before ruine the spirit shal be exalted. <na>[1]</na>
It is better to be humbled with the meeke, then to diuide spoyles with the proude. <na>[1]</na>
The lerned in word shal finde good thinges: and he that hopeth in our Lord, is blessed. <na>[1]</na>
He that is wise in hart, shal be called prudent: and he that is sweete in speach shal finde greater thinges. <na>[1]</na>
A fountaine of life the lerning of him that possesseth it: the doctrine of fooles foolishnes. <na>[1]</na>
The hart of the wise shal instruct his mouth: and shal adde grace to his lippes. <na>[1]</na>
Wel set wordes are a honie combe: swetnes of the soule the health of the bones. <na>[1]</na>
There is a way that seemeth to a man right: and the later endes therof lead to death. <cr>[1]</cr><na>[2]</na>
The soule of him that laboureth doth labour to himself, because his mouth hath compelled him: <na>[1]</na>
The impious man diggeth euil, and in his lippes fire burneth. <na>[1]</na>
A peruerse man raiseth contentions: and one ful of wordes separateth princes. <na>[1]</na>
An vniust man allureth his frende: and leadeth him by a way not good. <na>[1]</na>
He that with astoinied eies thinketh wicked thinges, byting his lippes bringeth euil to passe. <na>[1]</na>
A crowne of dignitie old age, which shal be found in the wayes of iustice. <na>[1]</na>
Better is the patient then a strong man: and he that ruleth his minde, then the ouerthrower of cities. <na>[1]</na>
Lottes are cast into the bosome, but they are ordered of our Lord. <na>[1]</na>
BEtter is a drie morsel with ioy, then a house ful of victimes with brawling. <na>[1]</na>
A wise seruant shal rule ouer foolish children, and diuide inheritance among bretheren. <na>[1]</na>
As siluer is tried by fyre, and gold in the fournace: so our Lord proueth the the harts. <na>[1]</na>
The euil man obeyeth an vniust tongue: and the deceitful obeyeth lying lippes. <na>[1]</na>
He that despiseth the poore, vpbraydeth his maker: and he that reioyceth at an other mans ruine, shal not be vnpunished. <na>[1]</na>
The crowne of oldmen the childrens children: and the glorie of children their fathers. <na>[1]</na>
Eloquent wordes become not a foole, nor lying lippes a prince. <na>[1]</na>
A most gratful pearle, the expectation of him that expecteth: whither soeuer he turneth himself, he vnderstandeth wisely. <na>[1]</na>
He that concealeth offence, seeketh frendshipes: he that in other word repeteth it, seperateth the confederate. <na>[1]</na>
Reprehension doth more profit with a wiseman, then an hundred stripes with a foole. <na>[1]</na>
An euil man alwayes seeketh brawles: but a cruel angel shal be sent against him. <na>[1]</na>
It is better to meete a beare when her yong are taken away, then a foole trusting to himselfe in his owne follie. <na>[1]</na>
He that rendereth euil thinges for good, euil shal not depart from his house. <na>[1]</na>
He that letteth water goe, is the head of brawles: & before he suffer contumelie, he forsaketh iudgement. <na>[1]</na>
He that iustifieth the impious, and he that condemneth the iust, both are abominable before God. <na>[1]</na>
What doth it profit a foole to haue riches, wheras he can not buy wisdom? <na>[1]</na> He that maketh his house high, seeketh ruine: and he that refuseth to learne, shal fal into euils. <na>[2]</na>
He loueth at al time that is a frend: and a brother is proued in distresses. <na>[1]</na>
A foolish man wil clappe the handes, when he is suretie for his freind. <na>[1]</na>
He that meditateth discordes, loueth brawles: and he that exalteth the doore, seeketh ruine. <na>[1]</na>
He that is of a peruerse hart, shal not finde good: and he that turneth his tongue, shal fal into euil. <na>[1]</na>
A foole is borne to his owne ignominie: but neither shal the father reioyce in a foole. <na>[1]</na>
A ioyful minde maketh a florishing age: a sorowful spirit dryeth vp the bones. <na>[1]</na>
The impious receiueth giftes out of the bosome, that he may peruert the pathes of iudgement. <na>[1]</na>
In the face of the prudent wisdom shineth: the eies of fooles are in the endes of the earth. <na>[1]</na>
A foolish sonne is the anger of the father: and the sorow of the mother that bare him. <na>[1]</na>
It is not good, to doe hurt to the iust: nor to strike the prince, which iudgeth right. <na>[1]</na>
He that moderateth his wordes, is lerned and prudent: and the lerned man is of a precious spirit. <na>[1]</na>
The foole also if he hold his peace, shal be reputed wise: and if he close his lippes, a man of vnderstanding. <na>[1]</na>
HE seeketh occasions that wil depart from a frend: he shal euer be subiect to reproch. <na>[1]</na>
A foole receiueth not the wordes of prudence: vnlesse thou say those thinges which are in his hart. <na>[1]</na>
The impious when he shal come into the depth of sinnes, contemneth: but ignominie and reproch folow him. <na>[1]</na>
Deepe water wordes from the mouth of a <na>[1]</na> man: and a streame ouerflowing the fountaine of wisdom. <na>[2]</na>
To accept the person of the impious in iudgement is not good, that thou decline from the truth of iudgement. <na>[1]</na>
The lippes of a foole mingle him with strife: and his mouth prouoketh brawles. <na>[1]</na>
The mouth of a foole is his destruction: and his lippes are the ruine of his soule. <na>[1]</na>

The wordes of the duble tongued, as it were simple: and the same come euen to the inner part of the bellie. <na>[1]</na> Feare casteth downe the slothful: and the soules of the effeminate shal be hungrie. <na>[2]</na>
He that is soft and dissolute in his worke, is the brother of him that destroyeth his owne workes. <na>[1]</na>
A most strong towre, the name of our Lord: the iust runneth to it, and shal be exalted. <na>[1]</na>
The substance of the rich man a citie of his strength: and as a strong wal compassing him about. <na>[1]</na>
Before he be broken, the hart of a man is exalted: and before he be glorified, it is humbled. <na>[1]</na>
He that answereth before he heare, sheweth him self to be a foole, and worthie of confusion. <na>[1]</na>
The spirit of a man vpholdeth his imbecilitie: but a spirit that is easie to be angrie who can susteyne? <na>[1]</na>
A wise hart shal possesse knowlege: and the eare of the wise seeketh doctrine. <na>[1]</na>
The gift of a man enlargeth his way, & maketh him roome before princes. <na>[1]</na>
The iust is first accuser of himself: his frend commeth, and shal search him. <na>[1]</na>
Lotte suppresseth contradictions, and betwen the mightie also it determineth. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Vse of lote to make agreement.

verses.text: Brother that is holpen of brother, is as a strong citie: and iudgements are as the barres of cities. <na>[1]</na>
Of the fruite of mans mouth his bellie shal be filled: and the offsprings of his lippes shal fil him. <na>[1]</na>
Death and life in the hand of the tongue: they that loue it, shal eate the fruites therof. <na>[1]</na>
He that hath found a good wife, hath found a good thing, and hath receiued a pleasure of our Lord. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: A wiues vertue is her best dowrie.

verses.text: The poore speaketh with supplications, and the rich wil speake roughly. <na>[1]</na>
A man amiable to societie, shal be more frendlie, then a brother. <na>[1]</na>
BEtter is a poore man, that walketh in his simplicitie, then a rich writhing his lippes, and vnwise. <na>[1]</na>
Where is no knowlege of the soule, is not good: and he that is hastie with his feete shal stumble. <na>[1]</na>
The follie of a man supplanteth his steppes: and he boileth in his minde against God. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Mans owne wil the cause of euil.

verses.text: Riches adde manie frendes: but from the poore they also which he had are separated. <na>[1]</na>
A false witnes shal not be vnpunished:& he that speaketh lies, shal not escape. <na>[1]</na>
Manie worshipe the person of the mightie, and are frendes of him that geueth giftes. <na>[1]</na>
The brethren of the poore man hate him:more ouer also his frendes haue departed far from him. <na>[1]</na>
He that purseweth wordes only, shal haue nothing: but he that is possessour of the minde, loueth his soule, and the keper of prudence shal finde good thinges. <na>[1]</na>
A false witnesse shal not be vnpunished: and he that speaketh lies shal perish. <na>[1]</na>
Delicacies become not a foole: nor a seruant to rule ouer princes. <na>[1]</na>
The doctrine of man is knowen by patience: and his glorie is to ouerpasse vniust thinges. <na>[1]</na>
As the roaring of a lion, so also the anger of a king: and as dew vpon grasse, so also his cherefulnes. <na>[1]</na>
The sorow of the father, a foolish sonne: and roofes continually dropping through, a woman ful of brawling. <na>[1]</na>
House and riches are geuen of the parents: but of our Lord properly a prudent wife. <na>[1]</na>
Slothfulnesse bringeth drousinesse, and a dissolute soule shal be an hungred. <na>[1]</na>
He that kepeth the commandement, kepeth his soule: but he that neglecteth his way, shal die. <na>[1]</na>
He lendeth our Lord that hath mercie on the poore: and he wil repay him the like. <na>[1]</na>
Nurter thy sonne, despayre not: but to the killing of him set not thy soule. <na>[1]</na>
He that is impatient, shal susteyne damage: and when he shal take away violently, he shal adde an other thing. <na>[1]</na>
Heare counsel, and receiue discipline, that thou mayst be wise in thy later endes. <na>[1]</na>
Manie cogitations in the hart of a man: but the wil of our Lord shal be permanent. <na>[1]</na>
A needie man is merciful: and better is the poore then the lying man. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Good wil to helpe the poore.

verses.text: The feare of our Lord vnto life: and in fulnes he shal abide, without the visitation most noysome. <na>[1]</na>
The slothful hideth his hand vnder the armehole, neither doth he put it to his mouth. <na>[1]</na>
The pestilent man being whipped, the foole shal be wiser: but if thou rebuke a wiseman he wil vnderstand discipline. <na>[1]</na>
He that afflicteth his father, and fleeth from his mother, is ignominious and vnhappie. <na>[1]</na>
Cease not ô sonne to heare doctrine, neither be ignorant of the wordes of knowlege. <na>[1]</na>
An vniust witnes scorneth iudgement: and the mouth of the impious deuoureth iniquitie. <na>[1]</na>
Iudgements are prepared for scorners: & hammers striking for the bodies of fooles. <na>[1]</na>
VVIne is a luxurious thing, & drunkenes tumultuous: whosoeuer is delighted therwith shal not be wise. <na>[1]</na>
As the roaring of a lyon, so also the terrour of a king: he that prouoketh him, sinneth also against his owne soule. <na>[1]</na>
It is honour to a man, that separateth himself from contentions: but al fooles medle with contumelies. <na>[1]</na>
Because of cold the slothful would not plowe: he shal begge therfore in the summer, and it shal not be geuen him. <na>[1]</na>
As deepe water, so counsel in the hart of a man: but a wise man shal draw it out. <na>[1]</na>
Manie men are called merciful: but a faithful man who shal fynd? <na>[1]</na>
The iust that walketh in his simplicitie, shal leaue blessed children. <na>[1]</na>
The king, that sitteth in the throne of iudgement, dissipateth al euil with his looke. <na>[1]</na>
Who can say: My hart is cleane, I am pure from sinne? <na>[1]</na>
Weight and weight, measure and measure: both are abominable before God. <na>[1]</na>
By his conuersation a child is perceiued, if his workes be cleane and right. <na>[1]</na>
The eare hearing, and the eie seing, our Lord made both. <na>[1]</na>
Loue not sleepe, lest pouertie oppresse thee: open thyne eies and be filled with breades. <na>[1]</na>
It is naught, it is naught, sayth euerie byer: and when he is departed he wil boast. <na>[1]</na>
There is gold, and multitude of pearles: but a precious vessel the lippes of knowlege. <na>[1]</na>
Take his garment, that was the suretie of a stranger, and for strangers take a pledge from him. <na>[1]</na>
The bread of lying is swete to a man: and afterward his mouth shal be filled with the grauelstone. <na>[1]</na>
Cogitations are strengthened by counsels: and battels are to be handled by gouernmentes. <na>[1]</na>
Medle not with him that reuealeth mysteries, and walketh fraudulently, and dilateth his lippes. <na>[1]</na>
He that curseth his father, and mother, his lampe shal be extinquished in the middes of darkenes. <na>[1]</na>
The inheritance wherunto haste is made in the beginning, in the later end shal lacke blessing. <na>[1]</na>
Say not: I wil requit euil: expect our Lord, and he wil deliuer thee. <na>[1]</na>
Weight and weight are abomination with our Lord: a deceitful balance is not good. <na>[1]</na>
The steppes of man are directed of our Lord: but who of men can vnderstand his owne way? <na>[1]</na>
It is ruine to a man, to deuoure saintes, and afterward to retracte the vowes. <na>[1]</na>
A wise king dissipateth the impious, and bendeth ouer them a triumphant arch. <na>[1]</na>
The lampe of our Lord, the breath of a man, which searcheth al the secretes of the bellie. <na>[1]</na>
Mercie, & truth kepe the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemencie. <na>[1]</na>
The ioy of yongmen their strength: and the dignitie of oldmen a gray head. <na>[1]</na>
The blewnesse of the wound shal wipe away euils: and stripes in the more secrete place of the bellie. <na>[1]</na>
AS diuisions of waters, so the hart of the king is in the hand of our Lord: whither soeuer he wil, he shal incline it. <na>[1]</na>
Euerie way of a man semeth to himself right: but our Lord weigheth the hartes. <na>[1]</na>
To doe mercie and iudgement, doth more please our Lord, then victimes. <na>[1]</na>
Exaltation of the eies is the dilatation of the hart: the lampe of the impious sinne. <na>[1]</na>
The cogitations of the strong are alwayes in abundance: but euerie sluggard is alwayes in pouertie. <na>[1]</na>
He that gathereth treasures with a lying tongue, is vaine and witles, and shal stumble at the snares of death. <na>[1]</na>
The robberies of the impious, shal draw them downe, because they would not doe iudgement. <na>[1]</na>
The peruerse way of a man is strange: but he that is cleane, his worke is right. <na>[1]</na>
It is better to sitte in a corner of the house toppe, then with a brawling woman, and in a common house. <na>[1]</na>
The soule of the impious desireth euil, he wil not haue pitie on his neighbour. <na>[1]</na>
The pestilent man being punished, the litle one wil be wiser: and if he folow the wiseman, he wil take knowlege. <na>[1]</na>
The iust deuiseth concerning the house of the impious, that he may draw the impious from euil. <na>[1]</na>
He that stoppeth his eare at the crie of the poore, himself also shal crie, and shal not be heard. <na>[1]</na>
A gift hid quencketh angers: and a gift in the bosome the greatest indignation. <na>[1]</na>
It is a ioy to the iust to doe iudgement: and dread to them that worke iniquitie. <na>[1]</na>
A man, that shal erre from the way of doctrine, shal abyde in the assemblie of giantes. <na>[1]</na>
He that loueth good cheere, shal be in pouertie: he that loueth wine, and fatte thinges, shal not be rich. <na>[1]</na>
The impious shal be geuen for the iust: and the vniust for the righteous. <na>[1]</na>
It is better to dwel in a desert land, then with a brawling and angrie woman. <na>[1]</na>
Treasure to be desired, and oyle in the habitation of the iust: and the vnwise man shal dissipate it. <na>[1]</na>
He that foloweth iustice and mercie, shal finde life, iustice, and glorie. <na>[1]</na>
The wise hath scaled the citie of the strong, and hath destroyed the confidence therof. <na>[1]</na>
He that kepeth his mouth, and his tongue, kepeth his soule from distresses. <na>[1]</na>
The proude and arrogant is called vnlerned, which in anger worketh pride. <na>[1]</na>
Desires kil the slothful: for his handes would not worke any thing: <na>[1]</na>
al the day he longeth and desireth: but he that is iust, wil geue, and wil not cease. <na>[1]</na>
The hostes of the impious abominable, because they are offered of wickednes. <na>[1]</na>
A lying witnes shal perish: an obedient man shal speake victorie. <na>[1]</na>
The impious man malepertly hardeneth his countenance: but he that is righteous, correcteth his way. <na>[1]</na>
There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against our Lord. <na>[1]</na>
The horse is prepared to the day of battel: but our Lord geueth saluation. <na>[1]</na>
BEtter is a good name, then much riches: aboue siluer and gold, good grace. <na>[1]</na>
The rich and poore haue mette one an other: our Lord is the maker of both. <na>[1]</na>
The subtel saw euil, and hyd himself: the innocent passed by, and was afflicted with damage. <na>[1]</na>
The end of modestie the feare of our Lord, riches and glorie and life. <na>[1]</na>
Armour and swordes in the way of the peruerse: but the keper of his owne soule departeth far from them.
It is a prouerbe: A yongman according to his way, when he is old, wil not depart from it. <na>[1]</na>
The richman ruleth ouer the poore: and he that boroweth is the seruant of him that lendeth. <na>[1]</na>
He that soweth iniquitie, shal reape euils, and with the rod of his wrath, he shal be consumed. <na>[1]</na>

He that is prone to mercie, shal be blessed: for of his breades he hath geuen to the poore. <na>[1]</na> He that geueth giftes shal purchase victorie and honour: but he that receiueth taketh away the soule of the geuer. <na>[2]</na>

notes.text: Better to geue then to take.

verses.text: Cast out the scorner, and brawling shal goe forth with him, and cause shal cease and contumelies. <na>[1]</na>
He that loueth cleanes of hart, for the grace of his lippes, shal haue the king his frend. <na>[1]</na>
The eies of our Lord keepe knowlege: and the wordes of the iust are supplanted. <na>[1]</na>
The slothful sayth: A lyon is without, in the middes of the streates I am to be slayne. <na>[1]</na>
A deepe pitte the mouth of a strange woman: he with whom our Lord is angrie, shal fal into it. <na>[1]</na>
Follie is tyed together in the hart of a childe, and the rod of discipline shal driue it away. <na>[1]</na>
He that doth calumniate the poore, to increase his riches, himself shal geue to a richer, and shal be in neede. <na>[1]</na>
Incline thine eare, and heare the wordes of wisemen: and set thy hart to my doctrine: <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Rules of wisdom are necessarie, profitable, and vpon practise found pleasant: rightly directing al our thougtes wordes and dedes.

verses.text: which shal be beautiful for thee, when thou shalt kepe it in thy bellie, and it shal flow in thy lippes.
That thy confidence may be in our Lord, wherfore I haue shewed also it to thee this day.
Behold I haue described it to thee three maner of wayes, in cogitations and knowledge:
that I might shew thee the stabilitie, and the wordes of truth, out of these to answer them, that sent thee.
Doe not violence to the poore, because he is poore: neither oppresse the needie in the gate: <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Care of the poore, because they are deare to God.

verses.text: because our Lord wil iudge his cause, and wil pearse them, that haue pearsed his soule.
Be not frend to an angrie man, nor walke with a furious man: <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Flee from euil companie which may corrupt thee.

verses.text: lest perhaps thou lerne his pathes, and take scandal to thy soule.
Be not with them, that sticke downe their handes, and that offer themselues sureties for debts: <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Auoide suretishipe, lest thou fal into distresse.

verses.text: for if thou haue not wherewith to restore, what cause is there, that he should take the couering from thy bed?
Trangresse not the ancient boundes, which thy fathers haue put. <na>[1]</na>
Hast thou sene a man quicke in his worke? he shal stand before kinges, neither shal be before the vnnoble. <na>[1]</na>
VVHEN thou shalt sitte to eate with a prince, attend diligently what thinges are set before thy face: <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Modestie and discretion at the table of great persons.

verses.text: and set a knife in thy throte, if notwithstanding thou haue thy soule in thine owne power.
Desire not his meates, in which is the bread of lying.
Labour not to be rich: but set a meane to thy prudence. <na>[1]</na>

notes.text: Mediocritie of riches, and contentment with meane state.

verses.text: Lift not vp thine eies to the riches, which thou canst not haue: because they shal make to themselues winges as of an eagle, and shal flie into heauen.
